planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic, seasonally wet soil in full sun; rufous mayhaw occurs naturally in flatwoods ponds and river swamps of the Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia, and south Alabama, and performs best where soil stays reliably moist through the growing season.

directions: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, acidic soil in full sun to light shade, siting trees in low ground, pond margins, or swampy depressions where they will not be short of water during summer. Crataegus rufula is the third and least-known of the Gulf South mayhaws, a naturally occurring hybrid intermediate between eastern mayhaw (C. aestivalis) and western mayhaw (C. opaca) that arose where the ranges of its two parent species overlap along the Florida Panhandle, southwestern Georgia, and adjoining south Alabama. The reddish pubescence on the undersides of the leaves, especially along the veins, gives the species its 'rufous' or rusty-hawthorn name and distinguishes it in the field from the two parent mayhaws. Like its relatives it bears clusters of small, bright red, tart pome fruit in late spring that can be substituted for eastern or western mayhaw in jelly and syrup making, and its dense thorny branching, showy white spring bloom, and tolerance of wet, flood-prone ground make it valuable both as a wildlife food source and as a fruiting tree for low, poorly drained corners of Gulf South landscapes that would sour most other fruit trees.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Native Hawthorns of the Southeast

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in moist, acidic soil; Saline blooms later than many western mayhaw selections, which helps it dodge the hard late freezes that occasionally damage the earlier bloom of other cultivars in Gulf South orchards, and it produces best with a second mayhaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, acidic soil, since like all mayhaws Saline is adapted to the poorly drained bottomlands and bayou margins of the Gulf Coastal Plain where conventional fruit trees struggle. Saline is a named western mayhaw (Crataegus opaca) selection valued among east Texas and Louisiana growers for its late bloom period in late winter to early spring, a trait that reduces crop loss from the late cold snaps that can wipe out the flowers of earlier-blooming mayhaw cultivars, with fruit following in late April to early May. The fruit itself is notably large and firm, with reddish skin over pinkish-orange flesh, and holds well on the tree without dropping prematurely, giving growers a wider harvest window than more fragile-fruited selections. Plant with a second mayhaw cultivar for reliable cross-pollination and expect the tree to begin bearing within three to five years.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Mayhaw for Gulf Coast
